body_markdown:
Steve Morris is on the cutting edge of drag-and-drive V-8 engine development, with his own line of water-jacketed billet aluminum engines. Capable of producing well over 4000 hp, they are the next evolution of the big-block Chevy. You’ll find these engines in some of the quickest and fastest drag-and-drive competitors. Morris engines[powered Drag Week’s first five-second pass](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/watch-steve-morris-tear-down-a-4000-hp-big-block/) as well as 2026’s overall winner. In other words, Steve knows his way around an engine. Still, each engine combination is different, and there’s always more to learn. Take this 540-cubic-inch big-block Chevy, for example.


In his latest video, Steve dyno-tests a 540-cubic-inch[Chevy big-block](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/epic-engines/a-rats-life-chevy-big-block-v-8s-thrived-for-over-half-a-century/) meant for a street-going 1968 Corvette. Steve points out the engine’s new Dart Pro 2 380 heads, which feature new, larger exhaust ports to help high-rpm power. The 380cc heads use 2.35-inch intake valves, 1.88-inch exhaust valves, and CNC-machined ports, bowls, and combustion chambers. These are serious heads that are not cut out for a 396. With enough displacement, however, they can really do their thing.


Although the engine puts up decent numbers on its initial dyno run, one of the big lessons from this test is that a high-rpm engine needs all the help it can get to deliver a powerful spark to light off the air/fuel mixture. In this case, moving from a typical dual-sync distributor to a more accurate crank-trigger and coil-near-plug ignition results in an engine that runs smoother and makes more power—just barely breaking the 900-hp threshold.


Even if you aren’t looking for a big-block that makes 900 hp on pump gas, there are lessons to be learned. For example, while this 8000-rpm big-block benefited from a crank-trigger ignition, this video also shows that a plain old distributor can offer solid performance on street engines at the kind of engine speeds that we’re typically used to.


What’s great about Steve’s videos is that he welcomes the viewer into his thought process. He also admits that he’s still learning even after decades of experience and thousands of dyno pulls. Besides some tips on ignition timing, Steve also shows how he adjusts the injector end angle using the Holley EFI software. For those who may not be familiar, injector end angle has nothing to do with the way the fuel injector is aimed or its spray pattern. Instead, the phrase refers to the angle of the crankshaft when the injector has finished spraying its charge of fuel. Getting the fuel injected precisely when it’s needed is an often-overlooked aspect of EFI tuning and seems to be worth the effort in this case.


Steve Morris Engines


Steve didn’t share the cam specs, but the solid roller that he had custom-ground for this street beast absolutely delivered. Not only does the engine churn out an impressively flat torque curve, but the engine power also has a plateau that lasts about 1000 rpm. A drag racer might be willing to sacrifice some of that broad power for the higher peak that a few more degrees of cam duration would deliver, but we agree that this is an impressive powerplant as-is.


This engine’s output of 1 and 2/3 horsepower per cubic inch is solid for just about any pushrod V-8, and that figure is particularly impressive for an engine with a moderate compression ratio of 10.4:1. Yes, that is a serious throttle body and a rather tall Edelbrock Super Victor intake, and nobody would mistake this for a sleeper, but what this engine really reminds us of is the importance of selecting engine parts that complement one another.
